title: Numeral Systems Across Languages Support Efficient Communication: From Approximate Numerosity to Recursion

claims.statement: Attested numeral systems (30 languages: approximate, exact restricted, recursive) tend to be more informative than most hypothetical systems of the same complexity, i.e. they are near-optimally efficient; the result depends on a need distribution that decreases with magnitude and fails under uniform need.
claims.scope: Numbers 1-100; need = English Google-ngram numeral frequencies smoothed to 0.6182 x^-2.02; complexity = symbols in a hand-written grammar; listener models grounded in subitizing / Weber's law / exact numerosity; evidence is visual (Fig. 3A), no test statistic.

quantities.name: placements_of_3_exact_terms_beating_the_prefix
quantities.unit: placements of 3 exact singleton terms on 1..100 (residual = one 'higher' term) with lower expected cost than {1,2,3}
quantities.baseline: same for k = 2 (0/4,950) and, in 20,000 random placements, k = 4 and 6; holds for a Bayesian and a uniform residual listener

quantities.name: need_mass_on_numbers_1_to_3
quantities.unit: share of total communicative need (paper's power law) on 1..3

our_assessment.why: For the largest class in the sample, the result is close to a tautology of the setup. 14 of the 18 exact-restricted languages are 'exact terms for the first k numbers plus one higher term'. Under the paper's own need distribution, which puts 84% of all need on 1-3, the prefix placement is the exact optimum: none of 161,700 alternative placements of three exact terms does better, under either listener model. Exact-restricted systems that count from one are therefore efficient by construction, and 'efficiency explains them' reduces to 'counting starts at one, and small numbers are needed most'. That second premise is estimated from English usage, which already has words for small numbers, and the authors show the result fails under uniform need, so the circle is visible. The hypothetical systems against which attested ones look good (Fig. 3C) are those with coarse low numbers, i.e. the systems that do not count from one. The structural null that matters -- 'any system whose exact terms are a prefix of the number line' -- is the attested class itself. Recursive systems (cost 0 by construction) and approximate systems are not touched by this check.

relations.why: Same programme and the same missing null: the class-defining structure (here, exact terms as a prefix of the number line) already delivers the efficiency under the assumed need.
Need distribution estimated from usage of the very terms whose efficiency is being judged (English numerals; WCS naming data for the LI prior).

open_questions: Retrieve OSF jmrqw when OSF is back: rerun their Fig. 3A comparison restricted to prefix-respecting hypothetical systems.

Does efficiency discriminate WHICH k languages choose (3 vs 4 vs 6) beyond the prefix shape? With cost falling monotonically in k and complexity rising, any k is on the frontier -- variation across languages is not explained by the model.
